newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ex-Soviet dissident writer Sinyavsky dies, aged 71.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Soviet dissident writer Sinyavsky dies, aged 71.

text.p: Russian novelist Andrei Sinyavsky, whose 1966 trial for writing "anti-Soviet works" is widely considered the start of dissidence against communist rule, died in a Paris suburb of cancer on Tuesday. He was 71.
"He died at home after a long illness," his son Yegor Sinyavsky told Reuters. "He was completing a novel."

Sinyavsky will be buried on Thursday in the south Paris suburb of Fontenay-aux-Roses where he lived in exile, first from the Soviet Union, then from a Russia he denounced as a colossal black market under President Boris Yeltsin.

Sinyavsky was arrested in the former Soviet Union in 1965 and tried for writing "anti-Soviet" works after the Kremlin discovered that he had published satirical novels in France under a pseudonym, Abram Terts.

He was sentenced along with fellow writer Yuli Daniel to seven years hard labour in Potma prison camp after a trial widely viewed as marking the beginning of dissidence against communism in the former Soviet Union.

After his release, Sinyavsky moved to France in 1973 with his wife Maria Rozanova and his young son, and took up a post as professor of Russian literature at the Sorbonne. He and his wife founded Sintaksis, a literary review, in 1978.
His most famous work, "Good Night", a novel loosely based on his own life, was published in 1984.
In an essay which appeared in the review Continent in 1970, Sinyavsky explained his reasons for dissidence.

"A Russian writer who doesn't intend to write according to the State's orders finds himself in the infinitely dangerous and unreal situation of an author...subject to tough measures aimed at punishing and destroying him.

"Literature has become a forbidden and perilous terrain which makes it that much more attractive, a sort of double-edged game or adventure that in itself embodies the intrigue of a fascinating novel," he wrote.

Born in Moscow on October 8, 1925, Sinyavsky fought in World War Two before writing a dissertation on Russian novelist Maxim Gorky in 1952. Assistant professor at the World Literature Institute of the Academy of Sciences, he wrote his first novel "The Circus" in 1955.
Sinyavsky published several satirical novels in France under his pseudonym Terts, including "The Renters" in 1959, "Lyubimov" in 1962 and a collection of essays in "Unguarded Thoughts" in 1965.

After settling in France, Sinyavsky continued to publish under his pseudonym, releasing "A Voice from the Chorus", his memoirs of the camp, in 1973, "In Gogol's Shadow" in 1975 and "Walks with Pushkin" in 1976.

Sinyavsky's works have only been published in Russia since the early 1990s, according to his son. His last book "Ivan le Simple" (Ivan the Simple-minded), about Russian folklore, was published in France in 1991.
In a 1993 article in a British newspaper, he strongly criticised the new Russia under Yeltsin.

"An enormous percentage of the population live on wartime rations and in the background of this mass impoverishment of society, mafia groups are making a fortune out of this colossal black market," he wrote.

He warned that "My old enemies have begun, occasionally, to speak the truth and my fellow Russian intellectuals have, instead of opposing Yeltsin and trying to correct the mistakes he and his team have made, welcomed the appointment of a strong leader and again call for strong measures to be taken."
"We have seen all this before. That was how Soviet rule began," he wrote.
